Guide

How to read an essential oil label

Last updated 26 October 2026

Two bottles both say lavender. One costs three times the other. The label usually tells you why — if you know which four things to look at.

The common name on the front of a bottle is the least informative thing about it. "Lavender", "cedarwood", "chamomile" and "eucalyptus" each cover several unrelated plants with different scents, different safety profiles and wildly different prices.

Everything useful is in the small print. Here is what to look for, roughly in order of how much it tells you.

1. The botanical name

This is the single most useful thing on a label, because it is the only part that identifies the plant unambiguously.

  • Lavender — Lavandula angustifolia is true lavender. Lavandula x intermedia is lavandin, a higher-yield hybrid, much cheaper and sharper, used widely in soaps and detergents.
  • Chamomile — Chamaemelum nobile is Roman, pale and apple-sweet. Matricaria recutita is German, deep blue and herbaceous. Not interchangeable.
  • Cedarwood — Cedrus atlantica is a true cedar. Juniperus virginiana is a juniper. They smell quite different and the second is far cheaper.
  • Sandalwood — Santalum album is Indian sandalwood. Santalum spicatum is Australian. Amyris balsamifera is not sandalwood at all, though it is often sold as one.

2. The part of the plant

Where a difference exists, it usually matters a great deal.

Cinnamon bark oil and cinnamon leaf oil come from the same tree and behave entirely differently — the bark is a severe skin sensitiser, the leaf is manageable. Clove bud is sweeter and rounder than clove leaf or stem. Bitter orange yields three distinct oils depending on whether you press the peel, distil the flowers or distil the leaves.

A label that says only "cinnamon oil" is leaving out the part that determines whether you can safely put it on skin.

3. The extraction method

  • Steam distilled — the standard for most essential oils. Heat and steam carry the volatile compounds across.
  • Cold pressed — used for citrus peel. Keeps the bright top notes, but also keeps the furocoumarins that make some citrus oils phototoxic.
  • CO2 extracted — pressurised carbon dioxide as a solvent. Closer to the smell of the raw plant, usually more expensive.
  • Solvent extracted — produces absolutes, as with jasmine and rose. Not technically essential oils, and some solvent residue is inherent to the process.

4. The chemotype, where it exists

Some species produce meaningfully different oils depending on where and how they grew. Rosemary is the one most people meet: the 1,8-cineole type is the one used in hair and scalp routines, while camphor and verbenone types smell and behave differently.

Thyme, basil and eucalyptus all have chemotypes too. If a label specifies one, that is a sign the supplier knows what they are selling.

What you can ignore

Grading phrases — therapeutic grade, clinical grade, aromatherapy grade — are not awarded by anyone and cannot be verified. The same goes for "100% pure" on its own: it is a claim every brand makes, including those whose oils are not.

A label that gives you species, plant part, extraction method and origin is making four checkable statements. A label that gives you a grading phrase is making one that cannot be checked at all.

A reasonable rule

Buy from people who will answer a specific question with a specific answer. If you ask where an oil came from and get a region, a method and a species, that is a supply chain someone is actually keeping track of. If you get a paragraph about purity and quality commitment, you have learned nothing.
